Job Description:

Job ID: 10758
Business Unit: MTA Headquarters
Location: New York, NY, United States
Regular/Temporary: Regular
Department: Information & Warehouse Mgt
Date Posted: Jun 17, 2025
Description

JOB TITLE:                   Manager, Product Development – Database Admistrator

SALARY RANGE:        $160,963 - $189,990

HAY POINTS:               805

DEPT/DIV:                    Transportation IT Products

SUPERVISOR:             Senior Director, Product Development

LOCATION:                  2 Broadway New York, NY 

HOURS OF WORK:     9:00am-5:30pm (7.5 hours/day) or as required           

 


This position is eligible for telework which is currently two days per week. New hires are eligible to apply 30 days after their effective date of hire.         

 

Summary:

This role is responsible for developing and maintaining product lifecycles from inception/innovation through design, build, and ultimately the ongoing run stage before an eventual product retirement. This role must possess knowledge in a core IT discipline and a broad understanding of related domains.

The role is also responsible for managing a team of database administrators (DBAs) assigned to design, build, and maintain one or more product lines. Various products including, but not limited to:

Corp Finance/ Capital Planning & Budget 
Legal, Risk & Safety 
Enterprise Asset Management  
Workforce Products (Payroll, Pension, Timekeeping, Recruitment)  
Employee Experience  
Platforms/Back-End Operations/DBA  
Bus & Paratransit 
Scheduling Crew Pick 
Transportation Intelligent Systems, Train Control  
B&T Products  
Customer Experience  
Revenue Fare Collections 
 

Critical Skills:

Strong knowledge of Oracle Database Administration
Peoplesoft experience (preferred)
Strong SQL Server experience
Cloud Data
Experience managing a team of DBA’s
 

 

Responsibilities:

Oversees staff workload and quality of work, addressing performance issues when needed.
Possesses knowledge in the database discipline and a broad understanding of related domains
Implements the product vision and strategy into the product development team’s work.
Identifies potential risks to the product and develops mitigation strategies. Escalates risks to leadership as needed.
Manages product initiatives are completed on time and within budget.
Manages through change including the ability to adapt to shifting priorities and market conditions.
Translates strategies and policies into operational plans, ensuring alignment with company objectives.
Delivers monthly or quarterly results, with performance subject to regular review against targets.
Collaborates with IT and business leaders to create and manage product roadmaps aligned with digital strategies.
Ensures team compliance with governance processes and adherence to technology architectures and methodologies.
Develops, manages, and monitors system support processes to maintain product quality and sustainability.
Understands customer needs, market trends, and the competitive landscape to inform product strategy and feature prioritization. 
Manages day-to-day operations and motivates team(s) to achieve results; may be responsible for a budget. Manages team priorities and resource demand/supply; recommends timelines and resources needed to achieve goals and objectives. 
 

Capability to lead, mentor, and manage a team of DBAs, fostering a collaborative and high-performance culture.
Supervises a professional team of IT staff in its selection, adoption, development, and support of one or more products lines through all stages of the product lifecycle, from ideation, definition, prototyping, design, validation & testing, launch, run stage, and eventual product retirement. 
Monitors and manages team activities and deliverables for adherence to relevant enterprise and departmental resource, technology, and operational governance/approval processes, and departmentally spanning technology architectures, models, methods, and tools. 
Analyzes and monitors effectiveness and efficiency of product(s), and develops, proposes, and implements improvement strategies. 
Develops and maintains personal knowledge of relevant industry models, methods, and tools, emerging technologies, and high impact regulatory changes.   
Performs other duties and tasks as assigned.
Observes the work performed by contractors.
Reviews invoices and approves them if the work has contractual standards.
Addresses performance issues with contractors when possible.
Escalates issues to other parties as needed.
Oversees rigorous quality assurance processes to deliver reliability, performance, safety objectives
Oversees staff workload and quality of work, addressing performance issues when needed.
 

Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities:

Technical Skills

 

Expert in deep understanding of technology. 
Strong ability to develop and implement enterprise product solutions. Ability to prioritize, handle multitask and work in an agile environment. Ability to quickly learn and understand new technologies. 
Strong experience with managing projects and initiatives. 
Strong experience with constant shifting needs and demands of the business Departments. 
Experience in at least one software engineering methodology, including but not limited to:  Waterfall, Agile, Scrum, DevOps, Extreme Programming (XP), Kanban, Lean, Rapid Application Development (RAD)
5-8 years of database management experience preferred primarily with Oracle and Microsoft SQL server. Experience with other databases is a plus.
Strong understanding of database technologies and architecture.
Hands-on experience of Backup Management and different Recovery techniques. 
Solid understanding of Disaster Recovery (DR), experience designing and Implementing DR and leading DR testing.
Proficient in Oracle database administration, including installation, configuration, and maintenance, database performance tuning, backup and recovery, cloning, patching. 
Strong understanding of database security best practices, ability to implement and manage security measures to protect databases and sensitive data within applications.
Understanding of industry standards and regulations, ensure the database platform remains compliant with internal and external process and regulatory requirements.
Lead proactive monitoring, tracking, and reporting efforts, as well as ongoing process and system improvements. Experience managing database-related projects, ensuring they align with business goals and are delivered on time.
Strong understanding of PeopleSoft applications
Experience with cloud database solutions.
Experience with the following vendor-specific platforms: OCI, Azure, Windows Server Linux, exadata).
 

 

Leadership Skills

 

At least 3 years of experience preferred in managing and leading teams on large scale projects and maintaining high performing DBA team.
Experience in managing incidents, on-call / shift rotation schedules, scheduled maintenance / deployment activities. Expert leadership in leading change by developing inter/intra team communication and cohesiveness; sustainment of culture and supporting staff during organizational growth/changes.
Expert leadership in leading people by working with staff to develop systems to ensure consistent, high-quality project management discipline for all technology related initiatives and endeavors.
Expert leadership in driving results by meeting organizational goals and customer expectations and make decisions that produce high-quality results by applying technical knowledge, analyzing problems, and calculating risks.
Expert leadership in business acumen by providing direction on evaluation, selection, implementation, and maintenance of information systems, ensuring appropriate investment in strategic and operational systems.
Expert leadership in building coalition by internally and externally building partnerships with key stakeholders to help achieve the MTA’s mission or common goals through influence or negations.
 

 

Behavioral Skills

 

Demonstrated ability to lead teams, provide coaching and direct feedback.
Expert in active listening, attention to detail, customer service, prioritization, and problem-solving skills.
Expert in working independently and strategically.
Expert in identifying and analyzing risks and developing effective mitigation strategies.
Expert technical knowledge and diverse skillset to understand various technologies, systems, and potential risks.
Expert in critical thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making skills.
Expert in interpersonal and verbal and written communication skills, with the ability to effectively collaborate with both technical and non-technical peers.
Expert in managing multiple projects simultaneously and prioritizing tasks based on urgency and impact.
Extensive hands-on experience with related tools.
Expert experience with working under pressure and meet deadlines individually and collaboratively. Thinks logically, assesses problems, and is results-oriented.
Expert in identifying complex business and technology risks and associated vulnerabilities.
Expert in communicating effectively, both orally and in writing, to interact with team members, customers, management, and support personnel (technical and non-technical).
Expert in establishing and maintaining effective working relationships with employees at all levels within the organization, and with both internal and external customers.

ROLE
You are my meeting note-taker for IT deployment / device integration meetings. Write like a competent project coordinator documenting for operational execution.

INPUTS I WILL PROVIDE
1) Raw meeting notes (bullets, fragments, messy is fine)
2) Any attachments or screenshots (slides, tables, photos of schedules)
3) Meeting metadata (date, facilitator, attendees if known)
4) Optional: known constraints (site rules, dependencies, exceptions)

NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES
- Do NOT invent facts. If something is unknown, write: “Not captured.”
- Do NOT mention AI, drafting assistance, or anything that signals automation.
- If screenshots/slides contain schedule tables or scope bullets, extract them and embed them into the document (as tables + sections).
- If slides and raw notes conflict, do NOT pick a winner. Record both and label “Needs confirmation.”

OUTPUT FORMAT (DARK MODE AESTHETIC)
Produce a polished, cohesive document with:
- Dark-mode styling (dark background feel, light text, blue headings)
- Clean section numbering
- Clear captions for tables (e.g., “Table 1. Schedule”)
- Footer with: <Project Name> | <Meeting Date> | Page X of Y

DOCUMENT OUTLINE (USE THIS EXACT STRUCTURE)
Title: <Project / Meeting Name>
Subtitle: Meeting Notes
Meta line: Date | Facilitator | Prepared by

1. Attendance
- Present:
- Participants:
- Others invited:

2. Agenda (from notes + slides)
- Bullet list mirroring the slide agenda when available

3. Scope and Summary (prefer slide text when present)
- Hospitals/sites in scope
- Device counts (anesthesia devices, perfusion, etc.)
- Locations (OR, Cath Lab, Endo, etc.)
- Standard workstation/cart kit (Cybernet, Neuron, scanners, etc.)
- IDT checklist (connectivity, vitals validation into systems, badge/scanner tests, cabling/labeling)
- Resource plan (teams involved: Epic clinical/technical, vendors, BioMed, anesthesia techs, PM)

4. Sites and Device Notes (site-by-site, highlight exceptions)
For each site mentioned:
- Current state (what’s already installed)
- What changes (hardware/software) are planned
- Neuron status: “existing / new required / none / unclear”
- Any contradictions or uncertainties → “Needs confirmation”

5. Schedule and Cadence
- Meeting cadence (weekly, etc.)
- Target completion dates
- Table: “W2 DI Update – Schedule” (extract from slide screenshots if provided)
  Columns: Location | Kickoff | Survey | Install/Test | Device Count | Comments

6. Resources
- Table: software packages / paths / owners (e.g., iPro package network path)
- Preserve exact paths; add line breaks for readability if needed

7. Staffing Plan (Contingency)
- Any “worst case” split or workstreams mentioned
- If staffing wasn’t discussed: state “Not captured; requires follow-up.”

8. Open Questions and Action Items
- Table with columns: Item | Owner | Status | Notes / Next Step
- Include “confirmations” needed from contradictions (esp. Neuron exceptions)

QUALITY CHECK BEFORE FINALIZING
- Every screenshot table is either embedded as a table OR explicitly summarized in the correct section.
- No invented attendees, dates, device counts, or site requirements.
- Every uncertainty is clearly labeled.
- Formatting is consistent and ready to send internally without edits.

You are my strict, evidence-driven Excel-for-Web debugger. High standards. No hallucinations.

Mission

Fix my workbook so the Printers tab populates correctly and stops being a graveyard. The logic must detect real printer tickets and exclude false positives caused by boilerplate text like “local printer installation”.

Files I will upload

My Tickets Tracker_OPS_WEBSAFE_DARK_PRINTERS_WIRED_MASTER_v2.3.xlsx (latest)

README — Web Excel Compatibility Rules - vNext.10.xlsx (rules)
Optional: screenshot of Printers still blank / false positives

Non-negotiable constraints

Must be Excel for Web compatible. No _xlfn.*, no _xludf.*, no volatile nonsense.

Do not invent columns. Use what exists.

You may add/extend an Error Log tab (keep it in final).

Anything you claim must be provable with sheet + cell references + evaluated results.

Before changing formulas, prove why Printers is empty/wrong using evaluated values (cached or via Error Log instrumentation).

Current wiring (assume this unless file contradicts it)

General!AV = _PrinterText (concatenated normalized text)

General!AT = _PrinterKey (row IDs of printer tickets)

Printers!N = _SrcIndex (enumerates row IDs from General!AT using a picker like SMALL/MINIFS/etc.)

All Printers columns are gated by $N2<>"".

The job (do in order, no shortcuts)
A) Prove the root cause (hard evidence)

Show exact formulas for:

General!AV2 (PrinterText)

General!AT2 (PrinterKey)

Printers!N2 (SrcIndex)

Provide evaluated values for:

General!AT2:AT50

Printers!N2:N20

Add to Error Log (if not already):

COUNT(General!AT2:AT1000) and COUNTA(General!AT2:AT1000) (type test)

_PrinterKey error count (ISERROR)

_SrcIndex numeric count (ISNUMBER)

Rows where AV contains "printer" but AT is blank

Rows where AT is nonblank but should be excluded

Acceptance proof: If _PrinterKey has no numeric row IDs, Printers will be blank. Prove it with counts and a sample slice.

B) Debug false positives (boilerplate contamination)

Find at least 3 false-positive rows (AT nonblank but ticket is not about printers).

For each row, show:

the full General!AV excerpt that triggered detection

which include keyword hit

whether it was only the phrase “local printer installation” or similar boilerplate

Add to Error Log:

a “Boilerplate phrase hit count” measure (exact phrase(s) used)

a “Strong keyword hit count” (zebra, print queue, not printing, label printer, etc.)

a per-row “Decision: PASS/FAIL” field

C) Fix the detection logic (minimal changes)

Goal: General!AT outputs row numbers only for real printer tickets in Excel for Web.

Rules:

PrinterText concatenation must wrap each component with IFERROR(cell,"") to avoid error poisoning.

Avoid fragile array patterns that Web Excel repairs.

Prefer scalar or Web-stable constructs.

Required behavior:

Treat printer as a weak keyword:

It must NOT qualify a ticket by itself if it appears only as boilerplate (e.g., “local printer installation”).

A ticket qualifies if:

It contains at least one “strong printer” keyword, OR

It contains printer AND does not match boilerplate AND does not hit exclude list.

You must implement and then prove it works using:

number of detected printer tickets

list of first 10 qualifying row IDs

demonstration that the 3 false positives are now excluded

D) Fix the extraction to Printers tab

Goal: Printers!N must enumerate the qualifying row IDs reliably.

Prove the picker works with evaluated results for N2:N20.

If the picker fails due to errors/types, fix it Web-safely.

Do not introduce AGGREGATE if it triggers compatibility warnings.

E) Deliverables

Upload the fixed workbook (new version number)

Validation summary (concrete counts):

Printer tickets detected (AT numeric count)

Printers rows populated (REQ populated count)

False positives removed (count + examples)

Update README rules with:

“Boilerplate contamination rule”

“COUNT vs COUNTA diagnostic”

Allowed/forbidden functions list

Stop conditions

If you cannot produce evaluated results from the workbook, create Error Log instrumentation so I can validate inside Excel for Web. Do not proceed without proof.

Optional attachments you may ask me for (only if needed)

Screenshot of tips include/exclude lists (B2:B200, C2:C200)

Screenshot of Error Log block showing counts

One false-positive row showing its AV text

Start by proving why Printers is blank/wrong with evaluated values. Then fix.

PUBLIC-LOCKDOWN REPORT ENGINE — v2 (DOCX + PHOTOS + RAID TABLE)

ROLE
- You are my STATUS REPORT ENGINE.
- Your ONLY job is to turn today’s context (chat + files + photos) into a PUBLIC-SAFE status report DOCX I can forward.
- Mode: PUBLIC LOCKDOWN — assume directors / PMs / vendors will see this.

CHAT TITLE
- When you infer a conversation title, use the format: “Task Tracker - {DATE}”.
- Example: “Task Tracker - November 21st, 2025”.

PRIVACY / REDACTION RULES (ALWAYS ON)
- NO: performance commentary (late, early, struggling, “problem techs”, discipline, access issues).
- NO: exact timestamps, shift times, clock-ins/outs, ticket IDs, IPs, queue names, drive paths, links.
- NO: PHI, MRNs, DOBs, SSNs, badge numbers, or anything patient-identifying.
- NO: quoting Teams/Outlook chats directly.
- If something is sensitive, silently generalize it.
- Attendance: If needed, summarize as “onsite coverage confirmed”; never list per-person hours.

PRIVATE LOG
- If a message starts with **“PRIVATE LOG:”**, treat everything after that as context ONLY.
- NEVER put PRIVATE LOG content into the DOCX.
- Do NOT relax any privacy rules for private notes.

NUMBERS, COUNTS, AND PERCENTAGES (STRICT)
- DO NOT calculate or invent completion percentages for anything (renames, overall project, rooms, etc.).
- DO NOT infer or restate numeric progress metrics (e.g., “86% complete”, “303 of 352 done”) unless I explicitly:
  - give you those exact numbers in the chat, AND
  - tell you to include them in the report.
- If I paste tables with counts, you may reformat them into Word tables using the exact numbers as given, but:
  - Do NOT add new totals or percentages unless I ask for them plainly.

STRUCTURE & STYLE (MIRROR PRIOR REPORTS)
- Match the layout and tone of my prior 200 Jericho reconnect reports.
- Sections (fixed order):

  1) Title block  
  2) 1) Executive Summary  
  3) 2) Outcomes & Wins  
  4) Rename Count — Daily Snapshot (ONLY if I give rename stats / table)  
  5) 3) Key Players  
  6) 4) Staging Evidence (Photos)  
  7) 5) Next Steps  
  8) 6) RAID — Risks, Actions, Issues, Decisions (TABLE ONLY)  
  9) 7) QC — DO NOT OMIT  
  10) Closing line

DOCX REQUIREMENTS
- Create a .docx and return a download link.
- Use Python + python-docx (or equivalent) in this environment.
- Page: US Letter, portrait.
- Margins: 0.75" all around.
- Body font: Calibri 11.

STYLES (MUST USE WORD STYLES, NOT NORMAL TEXT)
- Title line: paragraph.style = "Title"  
  - Text: “{SITE_PRIMARY} — Status Report (Reconnect)”  
  - 16 pt, bold.
- Section headers (1–7): paragraph.style = "Heading 1"  
  - Text examples: “1) Executive Summary”, “2) Outcomes & Wins”, etc.  
  - 14 pt, bold, dark blue (RGB 31,73,125).

KEY PLAYERS (PAY ATTENTION)
- Only list key players I explicitly mention in the chat for that day.
- Preserve the exact order I give.

  - Base them on the contributions I describe.
  - Do NOT invent duties, numbers, or impact statements that were not implied or stated.

IMAGES / STAGING EVIDENCE (PHOTOS)

  - `staged for tomorrow's workflow - TIOs and Ethernet Cables.jpg`
  - `Registration TIOs built out according to Seun's Updated Request.jpg`

  - “No photos provided for today’s snapshot.”
- If I forget to upload photos and do NOT say “No photos today”, ask once:
  - “Upload your report photos now, or say ‘No photos today’.”

RENAME COUNT — DAILY SNAPSHOT
- ONLY create this section if I:
  - Upload a rename-count file or table, OR
  - Explicitly type out a rename-count list and tell you to include it.
- Build a 2-column table under **“Rename Count — Daily Snapshot”**:
  - Col 1: `TDR`
  - Col 2: `Renames Completed`
- Use EXACT numbers I give (no additional math).
- Do NOT compute totals or percentages unless I explicitly ask for them.

RAID — TABLE ONLY (NO SEPARATE LOG)
- Under **“6) RAID — Risks, Actions, Issues, Decisions”**:
  - Insert a single RAID table (no extra bullet-style RAID log).
  - Table columns: `Category | Item | Impact | Next Step / Mitigation`.
  - Rows should reflect the Risks, Actions, Issues, and Decisions that I’ve described in the chat/files.
- Categories:
  - Allowed values: “Risk”, “Action”, “Issue”, “Decision”.
- Do NOT add narrative RAID bullets outside the table (the table *is* the RAID).

QC BLOCK (MANDATORY)
Under **7) QC — DO NOT OMIT**, include bullets:

- Photos embedded: <count>  
- Margins (in): T=0.75  B=0.75  L=0.75  R=0.75  
- Privacy filter enforced: ✅  
- Style check: Title style + Heading 1 style + Calibri 11 body applied: ✅/❌ (set accurately)

CLOSING LINE
- Final line of the report (plain body text, bold):
  - “No private notes included.”

WORKFLOW
1) Read this prompt (YOU ARE HERE).  
2) Wait for me to:
   - Upload photos (named files as above),
   - Upload or describe today’s tracker / rename counts,
   - Provide any extra context (PRIVATE LOG allowed).
3) Ask a single, short clarification message ONLY if something essential is missing (e.g., site name, date, or whether to include rename counts).
4) Use Python + python-docx to build the DOCX with:
   - Title style + Heading 1 for sections,
   - Bulleted sections in the fixed order,
   - Photo embeds + captions,
   - Optional rename table if I provide data,
   - RAID TABLE ONLY,
   - QC block + closing line.
5) Return a download link to the DOCX and do NOT print the whole report as plaintext unless I explicitly ask.

tasks.notes:
Start with the **parts that should survive your pivots** and keep everything else as replaceable machinery.

The mistake people make here is choosing React vs Vue or Django vs FastAPI too early. That is costume drama. The real architecture lives in:

1. **domain boundaries**
2. **contracts**
3. **data ownership**
4. **integration seams**
5. **operational rules**

If those are clean, you can swap tech stacks without burning the cathedral down.

---

# Approach

## 1. Separate the permanent from the disposable

Treat the system as two categories:

### Permanent

These should remain stable even if the stack changes:

* business concepts
* workflows
* permissions
* identifiers
* event names
* API contracts
* validation rules
* audit rules
* storage semantics

### Disposable

These can change with less pain:

* frontend framework
* backend framework
* ORM
* queue implementation
* auth vendor
* cloud provider
* search engine
* analytics tooling

That distinction is the skeleton.

---

## 2. Start with a modular monolith, not microservices cosplay

Do **not** begin with microservices unless you enjoy manufacturing your own suffering.

Begin with a **modular monolith**:

* one deployable app
* clearly separated modules
* internal contracts
* strict boundaries
* optional event bus inside the app
* later extraction only where pain proves it necessary

That gives you:

* speed now
* cleaner refactors later
* easier local dev
* fewer network headaches
* less distributed-systems nonsense dressed up as sophistication

---

## 3. Design around domains, not pages or tables

Your system should be organized by **what the business does**, not by controller folders and random database tables.

A strong starting split for your world would look like this:

# Core modules

## Identity & Access

Handles:

* users
* roles
* teams
* permissions
* auth session mapping
* audit of who did what

## Work Management

Handles:

* tasks
* projects
* tickets
* statuses
* assignments
* due dates
* dependencies

## Assets & Inventory

Handles:

* devices
* equipment
* kits
* stock
* locations
* movements
* status history
* assignment to people/sites

## Deployments & Operations

Handles:

* rollout plans
* site schedules
* work orders
* field execution
* completion evidence
* checklists
* deployment outcomes

## Documentation & Evidence

Handles:

* uploaded files
* photos
* OCR results
* generated reports
* notes
* extracted metadata
* document version history

## Automation & Rules

Handles:

* triggers
* workflows
* templates
* job execution
* reminders
* task generation
* rule-based transformations

## Integrations

Handles:

* ServiceNow
* email
* Teams
* spreadsheets
* cloud storage
* vendor APIs
* device management platforms

## Reporting & Analytics

Handles:

* dashboards
* export jobs
* KPIs
* trend views
* operational summaries

---

# The real structural trick

Each module should have **four layers**.

## 1. Domain

Pure business logic.
No framework junk.
No database calls.
No HTTP objects.
No SDK-specific types.

This is the brain.

## 2. Application

Use cases.
Coordinates domain operations.
Calls ports/interfaces.
Applies permissions and workflow rules.

This is the foreman.

## 3. Infrastructure

Database, APIs, queues, storage, OCR engines, email providers, spreadsheet adapters.

This is the plumbing.

## 4. Interface

HTTP routes, CLI commands, UI endpoints, webhook handlers, background job entrypoints.

This is the receptionist.

That pattern is boring in the best possible way.

---

# Foundational rule: ports and adapters

Every external dependency should be hidden behind an interface.

Example:

* `DocumentTextExtractor`
* `TicketingSystemGateway`
* `NotificationSender`
* `FileStorage`
* `IdentityProvider`
* `SpreadsheetExporter`

Your application logic talks to the **interface**, not the concrete implementation.

So later you can replace:

* OCR engine A with OCR engine B
* Gmail with Outlook
* local files with S3
* PostgreSQL search with Elasticsearch
* Django app layer with another backend

without rewriting the core logic.

---

# Suggested architecture shape

```text
/client
  /web-app
  /mobile-app        (later)
  /admin-console     (optional)

/server
  /modules
    /identity
      /domain
      /application
      /infrastructure
      /interface
    /work
    /assets
    /deployments
    /documents
    /automation
    /integrations
    /reporting
  /shared
    /kernel
      ids, time, result types, errors, base events
    /observability
    /config
    /authz
    /messaging
    /storage
  /bootstrap
    dependency wiring, startup, routes, background workers

/contracts
  /api
    openapi or typed schemas
  /events
    event payload schemas
  /integration
    external mapping contracts

/docs
  /architecture
  /adr
  /domain-model
  /runbooks
  /data-dictionary

/ops
  /docker
  /iac
  /scripts

/tests
  /contract
  /integration
  /e2e
```

This layout is not sacred. The point is that your **modules own their logic**, and shared stuff stays tiny.

---

# Shared code must stay on a leash

Most projects rot in `/shared`.

Keep shared code limited to:

* IDs
* time utilities
* common result/error wrappers
* logging/metrics hooks
* auth primitives
* message envelope definitions
* base config loading

Do **not** put business logic in shared. That becomes the cursed swamp where architecture goes to die.

---

# Data strategy

## Rule 1: each module owns its tables

Even in one database, ownership matters.

Example:

* `assets` owns devices, stock, location movement
* `deployments` owns deployment plans and completion states
* `documents` owns file metadata and OCR artifacts

Other modules should not reach in and freestyle SQL against each other’s guts.

## Rule 2: communicate via contracts

Use:

* direct application service calls inside the modular monolith
* domain events for looser coupling
* read models/materialized views for dashboards

## Rule 3: separate operational data from derived data

Keep raw data separate from:

* search indexes
* reporting tables
* dashboards
* caches
* OCR extracted text
* AI embeddings

Derived data can be rebuilt. Raw operational truth cannot.

---

# Event model

Even if you do not use Kafka or a message broker on day one, define domain events early.

Examples:

* `DeviceReceived`
* `DeviceConfigured`
* `DeploymentScheduled`
* `DeploymentCompleted`
* `PhotoUploaded`
* `OcrExtractionFinished`
* `TicketCreated`
* `TaskAutoGenerated`

Why this matters:

* lets you automate later
* lets you add async processing later
* lets you split services later
* gives you audit trails with cleaner semantics

Keep event names stable and explicit. No vague nonsense like `updated`.

---

# API design

Use three API classes:

## 1. Command APIs

Create or change state.
Examples:

* create deployment
* assign asset
* upload evidence
* run automation

## 2. Query APIs

Read models optimized for UI/reporting.
Examples:

* deployment dashboard
* asset status summary
* incomplete documentation report

## 3. Integration APIs

Strict mapping layer for external systems.
Examples:

* ServiceNow sync
* spreadsheet export
* Teams invite payload

Do not let external system weirdness infect your core models. Build an **anti-corruption layer** for each integration. Fancy name, practical point.

---

# Configuration strategy

Separate config into:

## Environment config

* URLs
* secrets
* provider choices
* queue mode
* storage backend

## Feature flags

* enable OCR pipeline
* switch notification provider
* use async export engine
* enable new workflow version

## Tenant or site policy

* site-specific rules
* deployment templates
* naming conventions
* required fields
* validation differences

This matters because policy drift is real. Hospitals, clients, sites, teams, all invent little goblin rules.

---

# Observability from day one

Do not bolt this on later.

You need:

* structured logs
* correlation IDs
* audit trail
* metrics
* background job status
* failure buckets
* retry visibility

At minimum, every important operation should answer:

* who triggered it
* when
* against what entity
* what changed
* whether it succeeded
* what downstream things it touched

That saves careers.

---

# Testing strategy that survives pivots

## Unit tests

For domain logic only.
Fast and numerous.

## Contract tests

For API payloads, event payloads, adapter interfaces.

These are gold because they survive framework swaps.

## Integration tests

Database + module wiring + real adapters where sensible.

## End-to-end tests

Only for critical flows.

The big idea:
**test behavior and contracts more than framework details.**

---

# Documentation you need immediately

Create these now, before the code jungle grows vines around your ankles.

## 1. Domain map

One page per module:

* purpose
* owned entities
* owned workflows
* dependencies
* public interfaces

## 2. ADRs

Architecture Decision Records.
Tiny documents for major choices.

Example ADR titles:

* why modular monolith first
* why ports/adapters
* why PostgreSQL first
* why event names are versioned
* why integrations use mapping layers

## 3. Data dictionary

Field meanings, allowed values, ownership, source system, validation rules.

## 4. Workflow catalog

For each workflow:

* trigger
* steps
* outputs
* failure handling
* audit expectations

This is the stuff that prevents future-you from fighting present-you in a parking lot.

---

# How to make stack changes cheap

Here is the practical recipe.

## To swap frontend

Keep UI consuming stable API contracts.
Do not bake business rules into the browser.
Keep validation shared by schema, not duplicated by vibes.

## To swap backend framework

Keep domain/application independent of framework objects.
Keep dependency injection/bootstrap isolated.
Keep route handlers thin.

## To swap database

Use repositories/queries behind interfaces.
Avoid ORM-specific magic leaking into use cases.
Be careful with DB-specific features in the core.

## To split a service later

Use module boundaries + events + contract tests.
Extract only the module whose pain justifies it.

---

# What not to do

A few traps, because architecture loves ambushes.

## Don’t organize by technical layer only

Bad:

* controllers
* services
* repositories
* models

That becomes spaghetti with better posture.

## Don’t let integrations define your domain

ServiceNow is not your business model.
Excel is not your ontology.
Vendor APIs are visitors, not kings.

## Don’t over-share the database

Nothing destroys module boundaries faster.

## Don’t build a generic workflow engine too early

Build 3 real workflows first.
Then generalize.
Premature abstraction is a well-dressed parasite.

## Don’t start with microservices

Unless you need independent scaling, team autonomy, or hard isolation now, it is just distributed confusion.

---

# A clean starting blueprint

If I were laying your foundation today, I’d start with this:

## Phase 1: architecture artifacts

Create:

* domain map
* module boundaries
* entity ownership table
* top 10 domain events
* top 10 API contracts
* top 10 workflows
* 5 ADRs

## Phase 2: repo + skeleton

Set up:

* modular monolith repo
* module folders
* shared kernel
* config system
* logging/audit
* test harness
* contract schema folder

## Phase 3: first vertical slice

Implement one complete workflow end to end.

Best candidate:
**evidence/documentation pipeline**
because it touches uploads, OCR, extraction, workflow, reporting, and integrations.

## Phase 4: second slice

Implement:
**deployment/task orchestration**
to prove assignments, statuses, templates, audit, and exports.

## Phase 5: third slice

Implement:
**assets/inventory**
to prove location movement, stock, association, and site-specific rules.

After that, the pattern will be real, not theoretical.

---

# Concrete module contract example

Here’s what “good seams” look like.

## Deployment module public interface

Commands:

* `scheduleDeployment`
* `assignTechnician`
* `startDeployment`
* `completeDeployment`
* `attachEvidence`

Queries:

* `getDeploymentById`
* `listUpcomingDeployments`
* `getDeploymentCompletionSummary`

Events emitted:

* `DeploymentScheduled`
* `DeploymentStarted`
* `DeploymentCompleted`
* `EvidenceAttachedToDeployment`

Dependencies consumed:

* `NotificationSender`
* `DocumentRepository`
* `AssetAvailabilityService`

That is crisp. No mystery meat.

---

# Tech choice guidance without handcuffing yourself

You said you want freedom to pivot. Good. So choose **boring defaults** for v1.

A sane starting set would be:

* PostgreSQL
* object storage for files
* one backend framework
* one web frontend
* background jobs
* OpenAPI or schema-based contracts
* containerized local dev
* monorepo or tightly managed polyrepo

But the deeper point is this:

**the stack should sit underneath the architecture, not define it.**

---

# My recommended first deliverables

Build these before writing much feature code:

## 1. Domain map

A table like:

| Module | Owns | Does Not Own | Publishes | Depends On |
| ------ | ---- | ------------ | --------- | ---------- |

## 2. Entity ownership sheet

For every major entity:

* canonical ID
* owner module
* lifecycle states
* source of creation
* key relations

## 3. Event catalog

For each event:

* name
* producer
* consumers
* payload schema
* retry rules
* audit retention

## 4. Workflow register

For each workflow:

* trigger
* actors
* steps
* outputs
* exceptions

## 5. ADR folder

Start with five. Keep each under one page.

---

# My blunt recommendation

Do this as a **modular monolith with ports/adapters, contract-first interfaces, event-aware workflows, and strict domain ownership**.

That gives you:

* freedom to pivot stacks
* speed to build now
* clean seams for later extraction
* less architectural theater
* more real leverage

The elegant part is not fancy tooling.
It is making sure the **meaning** of the system stays stable while the machinery changes.

Draft these seven modules on paper first:

1. Identity & Access
2. Work Management

7. Integrations

That exercise will tell you more truth than three weeks of framework debate.

ROLE
You are my Teams Invites Builder Engine for the “Active Teams Invites - TimeFix_NoWrappers” workbook. You output paste-ready cell snippets only. No hallucinations. No headers unless I explicitly ask. If any detail is missing, mark it as TBD and continue.

GOAL
Generate clean, readable invite content that technicians will actually follow. The invite body must:
1) Put the “BRING FIRST” list at the very top (Purpose) so it shows first in the Teams body.
2) Repeat the “BRING FIRST” list again at the bottom (Guardrails) so it is seen even by skimmers.
3) Codify the “+1 spare peripheral” practice: peripherals = device count + 1. Cybernets usually = device count unless I explicitly add a spare.
4) Enforce survey completion: technicians must complete the deployment survey before leaving the room, or deployment counts become inaccurate.
5) Use bulleted formatting inside cells where it improves readability (especially Hard Requirements, Stops, Guardrails).
6) Follow the real workflow for Stops: HQ pull → HQ verify/pack/label → travel → onsite stage/deploy → closeout/shortages. Do not invent generic steps.

INPUT I WILL PROVIDE (EVERY TIME)
A) Exact target paste ranges per column (examples):
   - Location column: I29:I30
   - Purpose column: L29:L30
   - Stops (in order): M29:M30
   - Hard Requirements: N29:N30
   - Suggested Timeline: O29:O30 (or times are elsewhere)
   - Guardrails: P29:P30
B) For each deployment row:
   - Site name
   - Date
   - Start/end time (or TBD)
   - Assigned techs (or blank/TBD)
   - Device count for that site
   - Any special notes (e.g., “Confirm two missing Cybernets with Tim”)
   - Stock lists (if already specified) or rules to derive them

1) Output ONLY:
   - “Range: <cell or block>”
   - A paste-ready snippet for that range in a code block
   No extra narrative unless it is a short “TBD/CONFIRM” note.
2) Lists inside cells must be presented like:
   • item

   • item

3) Purpose must start with:

Alright — let’s treat this like building a living, breathing “moral weather map,” except instead of barometric pressure, we’re mapping moral sentiment, ideological positions, and trustworthiness in real time.

Here’s a **breakdown for getting from concept to a functioning first version** of your platform:

---

## **1. Core Vision**

We’re blending **three systems**:

1. **Social Media Layer** – where people actually post, react, and interact.
2. **Trust/Source Scoring Engine** – to assess credibility and provide transparency.
3. **Moral & Ideological Mapping Layer** – to dynamically position groups and individuals based on aggregated sentiment data.

Think of it as:
**Public square + Fact transparency + Live moral/ideological map.**

---

## **2. Architectural Pillars**

| Layer                       | Function                                                                       | Example Tech                                  |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| **Client UI**               | Profiles, posts, comments, visual moral/ideological map, reputation indicators | React + Tailwind + WebGL/D3.js                |
| **App Logic**               | Posts, feed ranking, profile customization, comment threading                  | Django REST API / FastAPI                     |
| **Trust & Morality Engine** | Calculates trust scores and morality consensus; links content to sources       | Modular scoring scripts in Python             |
| **Data Store**              | Core accounts, posts, scoring metrics, moral dataset                           | PostgreSQL + Redis cache                      |
| **Security Layer**          | E2EE for messages, anti-bot systems, access controls                           | TLS + Keycloak/OAuth + device fingerprinting  |
| **Analytics Layer**         | Sentiment analysis, topic classification, misinformation detection             | spaCy, HuggingFace models, custom classifiers |

---

## **3. Major Feature Blocks**

### **A. Social Features (MVP)**

* Profiles (up to 5 personas per account, governed by trust score).
* Posting (text, images, video).
* Comments + emoji/GIF reactions.
* Customizable profile themes.
* Follow/unfollow, share, bookmark.

### **B. Trust & Source Transparency**

* Trust Score (identity, behavior, device, network modules — already outlined in your earlier spec).
* Source Score for articles/posts — shows where info came from, reliability ratings, and history of corrections/retractions.
* “Why this is rated” transparency widget.

### **C. Moral & Ideological Mapping**

* Axes like **Economic**, **Cultural**, **Libertarian–Authoritarian**, **Globalist–Nationalist**, **Technocratic–Populist**.
* Moral axes like **Harm/Care**, **Fairness**, **Authority**, **Purity**, etc.
* Positions based on aggregated ratings from users and trusted datasets.
* Live animation: group bubbles expand/contract or shift based on incoming sentiment.

---

## **4. Data Flow (How It Works in Real Time)**

1. **User Action** – A user posts content or reacts to a post.
2. **Content Pipeline**:

   * Text & media scanned for topic classification.
   * Sources (if linked) are fetched, analyzed, and scored.
   * Post inherits or is tagged with source reliability score.
3. **User Scoring Update**:

   * Trust score recalculated if the post or engagement behavior impacts credibility.
4. **Moral Map Update**:

   * Relevant moral & ideological positions shift based on aggregated sentiment toward topic/event.
   * Map visuals animate to reflect drift in consensus or polarization.

---

## **5. Safeguards (Your “Freedom + Facts” Balance)**

* **Freedom of Expression**: Minimal removal of lawful content.
* **Context Over Censorship**: Content gets annotated with:

  * Trust score of the author.
  * Source reliability.
  * Community moral consensus.
* **Misinformation Handling**: Instead of deletion, flag content with clear:

  * “Contested claim” badges.
  * Links to counter-evidence.
* **User Control**: Filters to hide contested content, low-trust authors, or certain topics.

---

## **6. Implementation Phases**

**Phase 1 – Foundations**

* Build Django + PostgreSQL backend with core models (Account, Profile, Post, TrustScore, SourceScore).
* Implement REST endpoints for account management, posting, and trust score retrieval.
* Seed moral/ideological dataset (start static).

**Phase 2 – Moral Mapping Prototype**

* Implement static interactive map (D3.js or Three.js).
* Feed it your seeded dataset.
* Create admin tool to manually shift positions for testing animations.

**Phase 3 – Sentiment & Source Integration**

* Connect NLP pipeline for sentiment/moral-axis classification.
* Integrate a basic source database (start with curated list, later expand to crawling).

**Phase 4 – Live Dynamics**

* Real-time updates via WebSockets.
* Batch recalculation of trust & morality scores every N minutes.
* Animate moral/ideological map based on latest data.

**Phase 5 – Privacy & Security Harden**

* E2EE for DMs.
* Rate-limiting & bot detection.
* Device fingerprinting and suspicious login flagging.

---

## **7. Early Dataset Approach**

Before users generate enough data:

* Pull from **Pew Research**, **World Values Survey**, and **Moral Foundations datasets**.
* Manually approximate ideological and moral positions for major public groups.
* Treat this as your “version 0” map.

---

## **8. Stretch Goal**

Integrate multiplayer games into the platform’s ecosystem — these could have their own trust/morality interactions (e.g., collaborative problem-solving boosts cooperation score).

---

If you want, I can next **draft the complete MVP database schema** that merges:

* **Social media features**
* **Trust scoring**
* **Moral/ideological mapping**

…so you can immediately start building in Django/PostgreSQL without guessing how the pieces connect.

Would you like me to produce that unified schema now?

Here's a summary of Theo's key points from the video, formatted for your notes:

Theo's Core Argument: Code is Not the Bottleneck (0:35)

AI coding tools are increasing code production (0:01-0:11), but not necessarily leading to more features or innovation in real products (0:21-0:24).
The actual bottlenecks in software development are not writing code, but rather:
Code reviews (3:12)
Knowledge transfer (3:13)
Testing (3:15)
Debugging (3:16)
Human overhead of coordination and communication (3:16)
Labyrinth of tickets, planning meetings, and agile rituals (3:21-3:26)
The Problem with Traditional Development Processes (7:01)

Long and Inefficient: Traditional processes (research -> design -> spec -> build -> ship -> pray -> deprecate) can take 6-18 months just to get to a working document (8:34-9:05).
Failed Assumptions: Bad assumptions made early in the process often go unnoticed until very late, leading to wasted effort and bad products (18:41-20:05).
Focus on Documentation over Validation: Too much time is spent on detailed specs and presentations rather than validating ideas with users (10:01-10:12, 22:10-22:20).
Shifting Burden: AI tools, when used within this old process, often shift the work from coding to more code reviews and reading long, AI-generated specs, which are often undesirable tasks (24:26-25:02).
Theo's Proposed Solution: Iterate and Prototype Fast (14:13)

Prioritize Learning and Insights: The goal should be to improve "time to next realization" or "time to next insight" (38:15-38:21). How quickly can you go from an assumption to a new learning?
Prototype Early and Often: Build throwaway prototypes quickly (3:06-3:08, 11:56-12:00) to test ideas with users (12:06-12:09) and get feedback before committing to a full build. This helps identify if an idea is worth building at all (17:00-17:01).
Iterative Process: Theo's preferred process: Identify -> Prototype -> Collect feedback -> Repeat until good -> Spec (short list) -> Build beta -> Collect feedback -> Go to five until great (14:14-14:36).
Distinguish Code Types: Understand the difference between throwaway code (for prototypes, experiments, quick insights) and production code (meant for long-term maintenance and solving core problems) (28:16-29:05). AI tools are excellent for generating throwaway code (31:18-31:21).
Empower Engineers: Use AI to free up engineers to focus on more enjoyable and impactful tasks like playing with new ideas, simplifying, and deprecating what doesn't work (22:50-23:07).
Better Communication: Smaller prototypes are easier for fewer people to discuss, leading to better communication and understanding within the team (40:41-40:49).
The Risk of Misusing AI Tools (26:19)

More Code ≠ Better Apps: Just as more words don't make a better law, more code doesn't make a better app (26:37-26:41).
Increased Verification Complexity: AI makes code production easier but makes verification more complex, potentially slowing down teams overall (27:19-27:24).
Diluted Quality: If AI-generated code is treated the same as production-ready code, it leads to more review burden, unfamiliar patterns, and unhandled edge cases (16:32-17:01, 27:50-28:12).
Misguided Pitch: AI tools are often incorrectly pitched as making developers faster, rather than enabling faster user insight and more effective iteration (39:59-40:08).
Conclusion:

AI's true benefit lies in accelerating the discovery and validation phases of product development, allowing teams to quickly learn what users truly need and build the right thing (20:51-20:59, 33:04-33:06).
Companies must rethink their traditional development processes to fully leverage AI's potential (25:17-25:21).

Here's a breakdown of the key points:

ATS Misconceptions (0:40): Many job seekers blame ATS for automatic rejections, believing it filters resumes based on keywords. The video clarifies that ATS primarily functions as a database for storing applications, not an AI that automatically rejects candidates (4:19).
How ATS Works (1:18): The speaker, an ex-Google recruiter with a background in computer science, explains that ATS uses optical character recognition (OCR) technology, similar to how the postal service sorts mail (2:04). It parses resumes for contact information to build a profile, but it does not auto-reject or auto-filter based on keywords (5:50).
Debunking ATS Myths:
Myth 1: ATS automatically rejects resumes for missing keywords (7:05). This is false; there's no hidden rejection algorithm (7:30). Recruiters rarely use keyword filters as they are clunky and often surface irrelevant candidates (7:53).
Myth 2: You need an "ATS-compliant" resume with a high score (9:18). This is a scam perpetrated by third-party companies like JobScan to sell resume audits. These scores are not real and are not used by recruiters (9:40).
Myth 3: The "white font trick" works (11:18). Hiding keywords in white font at the bottom of a resume is ineffective and makes you appear untrustworthy to recruiters (11:49).
Myth 4: ATS uses AI to screen candidates (13:25). Most ATS platforms are old legacy systems not powered by advanced AI. Companies are also legally prohibited from using AI for hiring decisions without serious compliance issues (13:50).
Myth 5: Rejection means the system filtered you out (15:17). Silence after an application doesn't mean a robot rejected you; it means a human recruiter, overwhelmed by volume, likely overlooked your application (15:54). Federal rules mandate that every resume is reviewed by human eyes (17:01).
What Actually Works: A Recruiter-Approved Framework (18:06):
    1.  Write for the reader, not the system (18:27): Recruiters skim fast, so make your resume scannable and immediately clear by front-loading accomplishments and using a clean layout.
    2.  Show business impact, not job activity (19:03): Highlight outcomes with specific numbers and results (e.g., "reduced churn by 14%") rather than generic job duties.
    3.  Bridge the title gap (19:36): If your current title doesn't directly match the desired role, add context or a one-line summary to connect the dots (e.g., "Product Manager (Functionally leading road map without formal title)").
Knockout Questions (20:34): While ATS doesn't automatically reject based on resume content, some companies use "knockout questions" at the application stage (e.g., "Do you require visa sponsorship?") that can lead to immediate rejection if your answers don't meet basic requirements.

The video emphasizes that the real challenge in job applications is to get seen, read, and remembered by a human, and clarity in your resume is key to achieving this.

Network deployment and imaging refer to the process of setting up and configuring multiple computers on a network, often in a business or enterprise environment. This involves installing an operating system, applications, and settings on multiple machines, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive if done manually.

Several technologies can streamline this process, including:

* **SCCM (System Center Configuration Manager)**: A Microsoft product that helps manage and deploy operating systems, applications, and settings across a network. SCCM allows administrators to create a centralized repository of software and settings, which can be pushed out to target machines.
* **MDT (Microsoft Deployment Toolkit)**: A free tool from Microsoft that helps automate the deployment of Windows operating systems. MDT can be used to create a customized installation package that includes the operating system, applications, and settings.
* **PXE (Preboot Execution Environment)**: A protocol that allows a computer to boot from a network location, rather than a local hard drive. PXE is often used in conjunction with SCCM or MDT to deploy operating systems and settings to bare-metal machines.
* **Autopilot**: A feature in Windows 10 that allows for automated deployment and configuration of devices, often used in conjunction with SCCM or MDT. Autopilot can help streamline the deployment process by automating tasks such as:
	+ Initial setup and configuration
	+ Installation of applications and settings
	+ Enrollment in management tools like SCCM

These technologies can help simplify the deployment and imaging process, saving time and reducing the risk of human error. They are commonly used in large-scale deployments, such as:

* Setting up new computers for employees
* Upgrading or replacing existing hardware
* Creating standardized images for specific departments or teams
* Managing and maintaining a large fleet of devices

By leveraging these technologies, organizations can improve efficiency, reduce costs, and ensure consistency across their network.

1. Decision Defaults (0:31-1:28)
Concept: Reduce mental fatigue by pre-deciding routine choices. This preserves decision-making energy for more important matters.
Practical Application: Identify your three most frequent daily decisions and create a default answer for each. Execute these defaults without thinking.
2. Environment Design (1:33-2:31)
Concept: Your environment significantly influences your behavior, often more than willpower. Design your surroundings to make good habits easier and bad habits harder.
Practical Application: Pick one habit to build and one to break. Redesign your environment to make the good habit at least two steps easier and the bad habit at least two steps harder.
3. The Maintenance Window (2:35-3:25)
Concept: Dedicate a non-negotiable 15-20 minute daily period to reset your life and prevent small tasks from accumulating into overwhelming chaos.
Practical Application: Set a daily alarm for your maintenance window. For 15 minutes, reset the parts of your life that tend to accumulate chaos.
4. Energy Accounting (3:32-4:25)
Concept: Recognize that energy, not just time, is a finite resource. Evaluate activities based on whether they drain or recharge your energy.
Practical Application: For one week, track your energy levels after every major activity (rate each task from -3 to +3). Ruthlessly cut or delegate tasks that consistently result in -3 energy levels.
5. Implementation Intentions (4:29-5:26)
Concept: Transform vague goals into specific plans using the "When X happens, I will do Y" format. This links a specific trigger to a specific action, making the behavior almost automatic.
Practical Application: Choose your most important habit and write down its exact trigger and action using the format: "When [specific trigger], I will [specific action] at [specific location]." Place this where you'll see it daily.
6. The Two-Day Rule (5:28-6:18)
Concept: Focus on consistency over intensity. The rule is simple: never skip two days in a row. This prevents the "all or nothing" mentality and builds resilience.
Practical Application: Pick your most important habit and commit to the rule: "I will never skip [habit] two days in a row." If you miss a day, the next day's action is mandatory.
7. Friction Elimination (6:22-7:13)
Concept: Obsess over reducing every extra step between you and good habits, and adding friction to bad habits.
Practical Application: Identify your most important habit. Count every current step to doing it and eliminate at least three. For your worst habit, add at least two steps of friction.
8. Temptation Bundling (7:16-7:59)
Concept: Pair something you should do with something you want to do. Your brain starts looking forward to the "should-do" activity because it's linked with a "want-to-do" reward.
Practical Application: List three habits you struggle with and three pleasures you enjoy. Create three bundles, ensuring you only get the reward during or immediately after the habit.
9. Identity-Based Actions (8:02-8:54)
Concept: Shift your focus from changing what you do to changing who you are. When habits align with your identity, they become effortless because they are simply who you are.
Practical Application: Rewrite your biggest goal as an identity statement (e.g., "I am someone who [behavior]"). Then, ask yourself, "What would that person do today?"
10. Constraint Liberation (9:02-9:48)
Concept: Limits create freedom. Adding specific constraints to vague goals makes action easier by removing the exhausting work of constant decision-making.
Practical Application: Take your vaguest goal and add three specific constraints (when, where, and how). Make it so clear that a stranger could follow your plan without questions.
11. Social Architecture (9:53-10:41)
Concept: You become the average of the people you spend time with. Design your social environment (both in-person and digital) to support your desired behaviors and goals.
Practical Application: List the five people you spend the most time with and assess if they support or sabotage your goals. This week, join one group or community aligned with your most important goal.
12. Progress Tracking (10:45-11:36)
Concept: What gets measured gets managed and improved. Tracking progress creates accountability and momentum, making visible the small, unseen gains.
Practical Application: Choose your most important habit. Get a physical calendar or a habit tracking app. Mark every day you complete the habit. Your only job is not to break the chain.
13. Reset Rituals (11:41-12:29)
Concept: Life will get chaotic, and you will mess up. A reset ritual is a specific sequence of actions you perform to get back on track when things go off course.
Practical Application: Design your reset ritual right now. What's the sequence of actions that helps you feel grounded? Write it down step-by-step and execute it when life gets chaotic.
14. Single-Tasking Systems (12:33-13:28)
Concept: Multitasking is a myth; your brain rapidly task-switches, which is inefficient and exhausting. Top performers single-task with intensity.
Practical Application: Tomorrow, block out one 90-minute window for your most important task. During that time, eliminate all distractions (no phone, email, secondary tabs) and track your accomplishment.
15. Maintenance Mode (13:31-14:34)
Concept: You don't need to be at 100% every day. Some days are for growth, but most are for maintenance—simply showing up to protect the baseline and prevent slipping backwards.
Practical Application: For each important habit, define its "maintenance mode" – the absolute minimum version you can do on terrible days. When overwhelmed, you're only allowed to drop to maintenance mode, not skip entirely.

The phrase "Cut failed changes by 30%" typically means to reduce the number of failed changes by 30%. 

In a business or technical context, "changes" often refer to modifications made to a system, process, or product. "Failed changes" would then refer to changes that did not succeed, which could be due to various reasons such as errors, bugs, or unintended consequences.

To "cut" failed changes by 30% means to decrease their number by 30% compared to a previous baseline or target. For example, if there were 100 failed changes previously, cutting them by 30% would result in 70 failed changes.

This phrase is often used in the context of quality improvement, process optimization, or reliability engineering, where reducing the number of failed changes is a key goal. 

For instance, if a company has a change failure rate of 10%, and they want to improve it, they might set a goal to "cut failed changes by 30%", which would translate to reducing the change failure rate to 7%. 

In mathematical terms, this can be represented as: 
Let $x$ be the original number of failed changes. 
Cutting failed changes by 30% can be represented as: $$x - 0.3x = 0.7x$$ 
Which means the new number of failed changes is 70% of the original number, or 30% less.


A "25% reduction in variance across sites" means that the variance, or the spread, of a particular metric or measurement across different sites is reduced by 25%.

In statistical terms, variance measures how much individual data points deviate from the average value. A reduction in variance indicates that the data points are becoming more consistent or homogeneous across sites.

For example, let's say you're measuring the average customer satisfaction score across different stores. If the variance is high, it means that some stores have very high satisfaction scores, while others have very low scores. A 25% reduction in variance would mean that the spread of these scores is reduced, so that the scores are more consistent across stores.

In mathematical terms, if the original variance is $\sigma^2$, a 25% reduction in variance can be represented as: 
$$0.75\sigma^2$$

This means that the new variance is 75% of the original variance, or 25% less.

For instance, if the original variance is 100, a 25% reduction would result in a new variance of: 
$$0.75 \times 100 = 75$$

So, the variance is reduced from 100 to 75, which is a 25% reduction.

import os, re, zipfile, tempfile, shutil
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from pathlib import Path

NS = {"r": "http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/package/2006/relationships"}

def fix_xlsx(in_path: str, out_path: str):
    tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    try:
        with zipfile.ZipFile(in_path, "r") as z:
            z.extractall(tmp)

        # 1) Fix absolute Targets in all .rels files
        for rels_file in tmp.rglob("*.rels"):
            txt = rels_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore")
            if 'Target="/xl/' not in txt:
                continue

            tree = ET.parse(rels_file)
            root = tree.getroot()

            # base dir is the folder of the source part (parent of _rels)
            # e.g. xl/worksheets/_rels/sheet6.xml.rels -> base = xl/worksheets
            base_dir = rels_file.parent.parent

            changed = False
            for rel in root.findall("r:Relationship", NS):
                tgt = rel.get("Target")
                if tgt and tgt.startswith("/xl/"):
                    # absolute target points inside the package
                    abs_target = tmp / tgt.lstrip("/")  # e.g. tmp/xl/...
                    # compute relative target from base_dir
                    rel_target = os.path.relpath(abs_target, base_dir).replace("\\", "/")
                    rel.set("Target", rel_target)
                    changed = True

            if changed:
                tree.write(rels_file, encoding="utf-8", xml_declaration=True)

        # 2) Fix transparent ARGB fills in styles.xml
        styles = tmp / "xl" / "styles.xml"
        if styles.exists():
            s = styles.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore")
            # rgb="00XXXXXX" -> rgb="FFXXXXXX"
            s2 = re.sub(r'rgb="00([0-9A-Fa-f]{6})"', r'rgb="FF\1"', s)
            styles.write_text(s2, encoding="utf-8")

        # Repack
        with zipfile.ZipFile(out_path, "w", compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
            for fp in tmp.rglob("*"):
                if fp.is_file():
                    z.write(fp, fp.relative_to(tmp))

    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(tmp)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    src = "Warehouse Tracker - Ledger Cleanup v2_websafe.xlsx"
    dst = "Warehouse Tracker - Ledger Cleanup v2_WEBSAFE_PATCHED.xlsx"
    fix_xlsx(src, dst)
    print("Wrote:", dst)

`$env:PSModulePath` is an environment variable in PowerShell that specifies the locations where PowerShell looks for modules to import. Modules are directories containing PowerShell scripts, functions, and other resources that can be used to extend PowerShell's functionality.

### What is `$env:PSModulePath`?

`$env:PSModulePath` is a string that contains a list of paths separated by semicolons (`;`). Each path in the list is a directory where PowerShell will look for modules.

### Default Value

The default value of `$env:PSModulePath` varies depending on the PowerShell version and the system configuration. Typically, it includes the following paths:

- `%USERPROFILE%\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Modules` (or `~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Modules` in PowerShell 7)
- `%PROGRAMFILES%\WindowsPowerShell\Modules` (or `C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules` on 64-bit systems)
- `%WINDIR%\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\Modules` (or `C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\Modules`)

### How PowerShell Uses `$env:PSModulePath`

When you run `Import-Module` or use the `#Requires` directive in a script, PowerShell searches for the specified module in the directories listed in `$env:PSModulePath`. The search is case-insensitive and recursive.

Here's a step-by-step overview of how PowerShell searches for modules:

1. **Split the path**: PowerShell splits the value of `$env:PSModulePath` into individual paths using the semicolon (`;`) as a separator.
2. **Check each path**: PowerShell checks each path in the list to see if it exists and is a directory.
3. **Search for modules**: For each valid directory, PowerShell searches for a subdirectory with the same name as the module you're trying to import.
4. **Find the module**: If PowerShell finds a matching subdirectory, it checks for a `module.psd1` file (the module manifest) or a file with the same name as the module and a `.psm1` extension (the module script).

### Modifying `$env:PSModulePath`

You can modify `$env:PSModulePath` to add or remove directories from the module search path. Here are some examples:

```powershell
# Add a new directory to the module search path
$env:PSModulePath += ";C:\MyModules"

# Add a new directory to the beginning of the module search path
$env:PSModulePath = "C:\MyModules;" + $env:PSModulePath

# Remove a directory from the module search path
$env:PSModulePath = $env:PSModulePath -replace ";C:\\OldModules"
```

Note that changes to `$env:PSModulePath` only affect the current PowerShell session. If you want to make the change persistent, you'll need to add it to your PowerShell profile or modify the environment variable system-wide.

### Best Practices

- Use the `Install-Module` cmdlet to install modules to the default module directories.
- Avoid modifying `$env:PSModulePath` unless necessary, as it can lead to conflicts or confusion.
- Use a consistent naming convention for your modules and directories to make them easy to find and import.

## Change-management jargon (plain English)

* **Documentation gates**
  Required artifacts before a change can move forward (risk/impact, test evidence, approvals, implementation/rollback steps). Used to prevent “incomplete” changes from reaching production.

* **CAB-style approvals**
  A formal review (Change Advisory Board) where stakeholders assess risk/impact, dependencies, and schedule. Output = approve / defer / reject with conditions.

* **Rollback plans**
  Pre-approved steps to restore the prior state if a change degrades service, including trigger criteria, time budget, and who executes it.

* **Incident linkage**
  Connecting incidents to the change record in ServiceNow so you can prove the change succeeded, or analyze if it caused downstream issues.

* **RCA / post-mortems**
  Root Cause Analysis after a failed change or incident. Fact-based timeline, true root cause(s), corrective/preventive actions, owners, due dates.

* **Runbooks**
  Step-by-step operational procedures: implementation, verification, rollback, comms, and handoffs. They make delivery repeatable across people/locations.

* **KPIs**
  Key Performance Indicators that show process health (e.g., change success rate, MTTR). You brief leadership on these monthly/quarterly.

* **Emergency change count**
  Number of urgent changes that bypass normal approval. Lower is healthier; too many suggests poor planning.

* **MTTR**
  Mean Time to Restore (service) after an incident or failed change. Measures how quickly you recover.

* **Backlog aging**
  How long change requests wait in each stage (submitted, assessing, waiting for CAB, scheduled). Surging aging highlights bottlenecks.

---

Use these as **resume bullets** (top of Experience) and as **talking points**. They emphasize **policy, process, scheduling, risk, and results**—with the tools as enablers, not the headline.

1. **Quality gates + failure reduction**

2. **Cross-site variance reduction at LIJ**

3. **Approvals, windows, and rollback discipline**

* *Résumé:* Facilitated **CAB-style approvals**, aligned **change windows** to clinical operations, published release notes and **rollback plans**, and enforced **post-change verification** with incident linkage in ServiceNow.
* *Talking point:* “My role was to balance risk and throughput—right windows, clear rollbacks, clean evidence.”

4. **RCA and prevention loop**

* *Résumé:* Ran **RCA/post-mortems** for failed/emergency changes; turned findings into updated **runbooks**, job aids, and retraining—improving first-pass success and lowering emergency work.

Under a copyleft license, anyone can use, modify, copy, or distribute the work—**but only if they preserve the same freedoms for others**, especially with derivative or redistributed versions.([opencontent.org][1])

* It **isn't the opposite of copyright**—it **depends on copyright** to enforce its terms.([GNU][2])
* Copyleft grants permission to use works freely—but **derivatives must remain free under the same license**.([TiDB][3], [Wikipedia][4])
* Common implementations:

  * **GNU General Public License (GPL)**: A strong copyleft license widely used in software development.([Wikipedia][5])
  * **Creative Commons Share-Alike (CC BY-SA)**: Extends copyleft principles to creative works like text, images, and music.([TiDB][3])

In essence, **"All rights reversed"**—you have permission to do as you wish, **so long as you pass on that freedom**.

---

## How to Cohesively Spread Information About Copyleft

You want to raise awareness about copyleft and its importance. Here are some effective and practical strategies:

### 1. **Educational Content**

* **Create approachable blog posts or infographics** explaining copyleft in plain language, perhaps comparing it to "all rights reserved" copyright.
* Include real-world examples like Linux (GPL-licensed) or Wikipedia (CC BY-SA licensed).([Wikipedia][6], [Alt Legal][7])

### 2. **Workshops & Talks**

* Host beginner-friendly workshops or webinars—introduce concepts, illustrate with examples, and guide participants through choosing or applying a copyleft license.
* Partner with universities, open-source meetups, or libraries (e.g., hosting a session at your local makerspace).

### 3. **Social Media & Visual Campaigns**

* Share bite-size explainers, myth-busting factoids (“Copyleft doesn’t prohibit commercial use!”), and share-alike badges.
* Use storytelling—highlight success cases of projects thriving under copyleft.

### 4. **Collaborate with Communities**

* Offer your content or workshops to **open-source communities, activism groups, or digital rights organizations**.
* Engage with the **free-culture movement**, which shares values with copyleft in pushing back against restrictive copyright.([TiDB][3], [Wikipedia][6])

### 5. **Practical Guides & Templates**

* Develop and share **license selection guides**—e.g., when to choose GPL vs. LGPL vs. CC BY-SA.
* Provide README templates that include proper copyleft licensing language—these help creators apply it correctly.([Alt Legal][7], [Number Analytics][8])

### 6. **Leverage Multimedia**

* Produce short videos or slide decks explaining copyleft—simple animations or visuals can make the concept more memorable.
* Consider collaborations with YouTubers or podcasters in tech culture or digital rights spaces.

### 7. **Leverage Existing Free Culture Efforts**

* Tie your efforts into broader **free culture** or **open access** initiatives to make the message resonate beyond software circles.([opencontent.org][1], [Wikipedia][6])

---

### Sample Plan to Launch the Initiative

| Phase                            | What to Do                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **1. Define Your Focus**         | Choose your audience—e.g., artists, educators, tech developers—and tailor your message accordingly.                                        |
| **2. Create Core Content**       | Write a clear explainer, design eye-catching visuals, and draft practical templates (e.g., “Apply this CC BY-SA license to your project”). |
| **3. Choose Channels**           | Use platforms like a blog, Twitter/X, LinkedIn (especially relevant for your link), and relevant forums (e.g., r/opensource).              |
| **4. Partner & Distribute**      | Collaborate with local tech communities or digital-rights groups. Offer guest posts, workshops, or social media cross-promotion.           |
| **5. Reinforce with Multimedia** | Launch a short animated video or visual slideshow that breaks down copyleft. Share widely and encourage reposts.                           |
| **6. Encourage Action**          | Invite accounts to pledge: “I’ll share my project using a copyleft license.” Use hashtags like #ShareWhatYouMake #AllRightsReversed.       |
| **7. Evaluate & Expand**         | Track engagement and feedback. If effective, explore translations, guest speakers, or longer courses.                                      |

---

### Final Thoughts

Copyleft harnesses legal structure to cultivate collaboration, not restrict it. It ensures that works—and their derivatives—remain open and accessible for everyone. By simplifying the message, offering practical tools, and sharing it across media and communities, you can help the public appreciate both its philosophy and its practical value.

Based on your constraints and goals, here are several approaches to discover print servers and queue names:

## VBS Network Discovery Approach

### 1. SNMP Query for Printer Details
```vbs
' Get printer system name and description via SNMP
Set objSNMP = CreateObject("SnmpAPI.SnmpMgr")
Set objExcel = CreateObject("Excel.Application")

Function GetPrinterInfo(strIP)
    Dim sysName, sysDescr, hrDeviceDescr
    
    ' System name (often shows print server or queue)
    sysName = objSNMP.SnmpGet(strIP, "public", "1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0")
    ' System description
    sysDescr = objSNMP.SnmpGet(strIP, "public", "1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0")
    ' HR Device Description (printer-specific)
    hrDeviceDescr = objSNMP.SnmpGet(strIP, "public", "1.3.6.1.2.1.25.3.2.1.3.1")
    
    GetPrinterInfo = sysName & "|" & sysDescr & "|" & hrDeviceDescr
End Function
```

### 2. Print Spooler Discovery
```vbs
' Scan for print servers and enumerate their queues
Set objWMI = GetObject("winmgmts:")
Set colComputers = objWMI.ExecQuery("SELECT * FROM Win32_ComputerSystem")

Function FindPrintQueues(strServerIP)
    Dim strServer, objWMIPrint, colPrinters
    
    ' Try to connect to print spooler service
    On Error Resume Next
    strServer = GetServerNameFromIP(strServerIP)
    
    Set objWMIPrint = GetObject("winmgmts:\\" & strServer & "\root\cimv2")
    Set colPrinters = objWMIPrint.ExecQuery("SELECT * FROM Win32_Printer")
    
    For Each objPrinter In colPrinters
        If InStr(objPrinter.PortName, strServerIP) > 0 Then
            WScript.Echo "Queue: " & objPrinter.Name & " | Port: " & objPrinter.PortName
        End If
    Next
End Function
```

### 3. Registry-Based Queue Discovery
```vbs
' Search print server registries for queue configurations
Function GetPrintQueuesFromRegistry(strServer)
    Const HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE = &H80000002
    Set objRegistry = GetObject("winmgmts:\\" & strServer & "\root\default:StdRegProv")
    
    strKeyPath = "SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Printers"
    objRegistry.EnumKey HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, strKeyPath, arrSubKeys
    
    For Each strSubKey In arrSubKeys
        strValuePath = strKeyPath & "\" & strSubKey
        objRegistry.GetStringValue HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, strValuePath & "\Port", strPort
        
        ' Check if port matches our IP addresses
        WScript.Echo "Printer: " & strSubKey & " | Port: " & strPort
    Next
End Function
```

## Network Scanning Alternatives

### 4. Batch + NMAP Approach
```batch
@echo off
REM Scan for print services and SNMP
FOR /F "tokens=*" %%i IN (ip_list.txt) DO (
    echo Scanning %%i...
    nmap -p 515,631,9100,161 %%i > scan_%%i.txt
    
    REM Get SNMP system info
    snmpwalk -v2c -c public %%i 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0 >> snmp_%%i.txt
)
```

### 5. Python Alternative (if allowed)
```python
import socket, subprocess, openpyxl
from pysnmp.hlapi import *

def discover_print_info(ip_address):
    results = {}
    
    # SNMP system name query
    try:
        for (errorIndication, errorStatus, errorIndex, varBinds) in nextCmd(
            SnmpEngine(),
            CommunityData('public'),
            UdpTransportTarget((ip_address, 161)),
            ContextData(),
            ObjectType(ObjectIdentity('1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0')),
            lexicographicMode=False):
            
            if errorIndication or errorStatus:
                break
            
            for varBind in varBinds:
                results['sysName'] = str(varBind[1])
    except:
        pass
    
    # Port scanning for print services
    common_print_ports = [515, 631, 9100, 445]
    for port in common_print_ports:
        try:
            sock = socket.create_connection((ip_address, port), timeout=3)
            results[f'port_{port}'] = 'open'
            sock.close()
        except:
            results[f'port_{port}'] = 'closed'
    
    return results
```

## Recommended Approach

1. **Start with SNMP queries** (VBS script #1) - Most printers respond to basic SNMP
2. **Cross-reference with network scanning** to find print servers
3. **Use the server discovery** (VBS script #2) to enumerate queues
